sum: JPMorgan has reaffirmed its bullish stance on Siemens, keeping an "Overweight" rating and a €345 price target after a conversation with the conglomerate's finance chief, Veronika Bienert. Analyst Phil Buller pointed to end-market momentum and market-share gains as the pillars underpinning the group's guidance for the coming fiscal year — a case that rests on Siemens converting that demand into actual revenue and profit.

The target sits well above Friday's closing price of €280.00, implying the stock has room to run if the operational story holds. Buller described the latest set of results, discussed during a webcast following their release, as either in line with or better than usual, and he had already flagged in a Thursday note that the fiscal 2027 outlook topped market expectations.

Siemens used the occasion to lift its mid-term growth ambitions. Earnings per share before purchase price allocation (EPS before PPA) are now expected to grow at a double-digit percentage rate over the medium term, up from a previously targeted high single-digit increase. Comparable revenue growth is now guided at 7–11%, widened from an earlier 6–9% corridor — a combination the company says pairs a bolder profit goal with a higher growth band for the business.

For fiscal 2027 specifically, Siemens projects comparable revenue growth of 9–11% and EPS before PPA of €10.20–10.80. According to Reuters, the fiscal 2026/27 revenue outlook refers to Siemens excluding Healthineers, with the spin-off slated for May.

The numbers released Thursday make plain how powerful demand for data-center equipment has become: orders in that segment doubled in the final quarter of fiscal 2026, with roughly €7 billion of the order backlog tied to the business. Chief executive Roland Busch sees no worrying slowdown in data centers over the coming years. Infrastructure contracts and automation are lending support alongside that unit, giving the growth thesis reach beyond any single end market — provided those activities keep their momentum.

On Tuesday, Siemens signed an agreement to acquire Lauterbach, a provider of debug and trace solutions for embedded software and SoC architectures, in a bid to broaden its offering for semiconductor design and verification.

sum: Siemens Healthineers closed fiscal 2026 with a strong fourth quarter, but its profit outlook for the new year remains below the result just achieved. The company reported the figures on November 5 for the fiscal year ended September 30, while an Ad Hoc News analysis on November 12 highlighted the mixed analyst signal.

Siemens Healthineers reported 4.0 percent comparable revenue growth for fiscal 2026 and an adjusted EBIT margin of 16.2 percent. Fourth-quarter comparable revenue growth accelerated to 5.9 percent, led by Imaging, where comparable revenue increased 10.0 percent. Diagnostics moved in the opposite direction, with comparable revenue down 4.2 percent and an adjusted EBIT margin of 5.4 percent.

The company expects comparable revenue to grow between 4.0 and 5.0 percent in fiscal 2027. Adjusted basic earnings per share are forecast in a range of 2.20 to 2.40 euros, below the 2.42 euros achieved in fiscal 2026. The proposed dividend remains unchanged at 1.00 euro per share.

Goldman Sachs raised its price target to 49 euros from 43 euros and retained a Neutral rating. Deutsche Bank Research lifted its target to 43 euros from 39 euros and kept its Hold rating. The target increases improve the valuation signal, but the unchanged recommendations show that analysts still want clearer evidence of an earnings recovery.

The main operational test is Diagnostics. Siemens Healthineers is preparing the in-vitro diagnostics business for a standalone structure under the Olyrian Diagnostics name, with the transition expected to be completed by mid-2028. Management is also positioning the core portfolio for stronger growth while preparing a name change to Healthineers as part of the planned separation from Siemens.

Siemens Healthineers stock traded at 43.72 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 11:33 CET on Friday, November 13, 0.18 percent below the Xetra close of Thursday. The contrast between higher analyst targets and guidance below the prior year's earnings leaves the shares dependent on execution in Imaging, cost savings and the Diagnostics turnaround.

sum: Investing.com -- Siemens AG (ETR:SIEGn) shares climbed to an 11-week high on Thursday after the industrial group reported better-than-expected quarterly results and raised its medium-term growth targets, as strong demand for AI-related data centre equipment and rail contracts drove record orders.

Shares rose 4.44% to €289.30, after touching an intraday high of €291.45, their highest level since August 28. The stock outperformed Germany's benchmark DAX, which gained around 0.9% during the session.

Net income for the quarter ended September 30 rose to €2.43 billion from €1.84 billion a year earlier. Revenue increased 11% to €23.68 billion, while profit at its Industrial Business climbed 22% to a record €3.90 billion. The industrial profit margin improved to 16.8% from 15.3%.
Orders surged 58% to a quarterly record €34.77 billion, lifting Siemens' book-to-bill ratio to 1.47 and its order backlog to €143 billion.

Growth was led by Smart Infrastructure and Mobility, reflecting sustained investment in electrification, digital infrastructure and rail transportation. Smart Infrastructure's revenue rose 16% to €7.24 billion, with order intake jumping 40%, supported by large data centre contract wins, particularly in the U.S. and Europe.

Digital Industries also delivered stronger results, with revenue up 11% and profit increasing 50%, driven primarily by operational improvements in automation. Mobility's orders more than quadrupled, supported by major German rail contracts, including a €2.4 billion high-speed train order.

Looking ahead, Siemens expects comparable revenue growth of 9% to 11% in fiscal 2027 and earnings per share before purchase price allocation accounting (EPS pre PPA) of €10.20 to €10.80. The company cited continued investment in AI and digital infrastructure, public investment programmes and a recovery in industrial activity as key growth drivers.

sum: Siemens Energy's latest buyback disclosure landed yesterday, and it does more than update a running share count. The company confirmed it repurchased 1,539,908 of its own shares in the 2–8 November window, its seventh interim notification since the programme began. Since the 24 September launch, cumulative purchases have reached 7,390,216 shares.

The stock, meanwhile, climbed 6.2% as equity markets broadly recovered. Media reports credited falling oil prices and the wider rally with supporting the DAX at the start of the week, with Siemens Energy singled out as a beneficiary of AI-related investment and among the day's gainers ahead of its annual results. The shares closed yesterday at €124.48.

With capital already flowing back to shareholders, the question weighing on investors ahead of the figures is whether expected cash generation can sustain those returns. Siemens Energy is targeting free cash flow before tax of around €8bn, alongside a profit goal of roughly €4bn — two figures that together sketch the financial capacity the group intends to reach.

That makes the inflow of funds the metric to watch. It links operating performance to the room available for capital returns, and the buyback case would rest on firmer ground if the cash flow target is met and the company can convincingly explain why its financial strength should hold beyond the reporting period.

On the operating side, full-year targets call for revenue growth of 14–16%, with the margin before special items at the upper end of a 10–12% range. Investors will want to see whether growth and profitability are pulling in the same direction to underpin the expected cash inflow. Announced targets alone won't earn a favourable verdict — delivery is what counts, and the more persuasively Siemens Energy ties business development to cash generation, the more credible the prospect of further returns becomes.

The bullish scenario leans on continued profit growth. Analysts forecast earnings per share of €6.30 for 2027, up from an estimated €4.48 for 2026 — projections that assume substantial further progress. Supporting that view, earnings estimates have been revised higher recently, rising 4.4% over the past 90 days, and Siemens Energy has beaten profit expectations in five of the last six quarters.

sum: Siemens will ask shareholders of both Siemens and Siemens Healthineers to sign off on the separation of its healthcare arm at their respective annual general meetings in February 2027, with the spin-off itself slated for 2027. The healthcare unit is to be renamed Healthineers as part of the carve-out. The announcement came on Thursday, a day when the industrial group's shares were caught in a broad global selloff across AI and semiconductor stocks.

The stock fell 2.9% on the day. Reuters linked the retreat to worries about tighter AI regulation following the US Democrats' victory in the midterm elections, and investors also fretted that the build-out of data centers could slow. The report framed the selling as a drag on the German equity market.

Separately, Siemens opened a new rail infrastructure technology and innovation center in Chippenham, backing the site with a EUR 115 million investment and citing 800 local employees. On the same day, Deutsche Bank Research reaffirmed its "Hold" rating on Siemens and kept its price target at EUR 270. Analyst Gael de-Bray pointed to somewhat mixed signals from competitors' automation results, while highlighting the company's still-strong order momentum in electrification.

Morningstar, for its part, puts fair value at EUR 240 — below the previous day's close of EUR 262.35. The research house assigns the stock a two-star rating, credits Siemens with a wide economic moat and classifies uncertainty as medium. For investors, the question is whether data centers and an expected recovery in automation can add enough momentum to justify the price.

Morningstar places triple-digit revenue growth in the data center business front and center. Demand for AI data centers and electrification stands to benefit Smart Infrastructure in particular — a positive for Siemens provided that strong demand feeds through to the broader business. For fiscal 2027, the firm expects organic revenue growth of roughly 8%, with Smart Infrastructure contributing the largest share. At Digital Industries, it is banking on a cyclical recovery in automation.
That leaves growth resting on two distinct drivers: infrastructure expansion at Smart Infrastructure and a hoped-for economic pickup at Digital Industries.

sum: Siemens Energy drew fresh support from two major brokers this week, with JPMorgan and UBS both reaffirming bullish stances just days before the company is due to report full-year results. The stock closed Friday up 3.8% at EUR 117.20, a rare bright spot on a day when the DAX fell sharply, according to dts.

JPMorgan kept its "Overweight" rating and a EUR 245 price target. Analyst Phil Buller pointed to an investor survey showing muted expectations ahead of the upcoming quarterly report and the capital markets day. UBS had already confirmed its "Buy" rating and EUR 210 target on Wednesday, with analyst Christopher Leonard arguing that the stock's losses during the sector-wide selloff were unjustified.

The rebound comes after a difficult stretch. Over the past seven days the shares are still down 7.3%. Media reports attributed the prior pressure to worries about stricter US rules for AI data centres and a generally weaker equity market mood. Siemens Energy was singled out as particularly sensitive to news on AI data centres because it supplies key customers in that industry, and the concern was that tighter regulation could hit those clients.

The Südwest Presse reported Thursday that fears over AI regulation and the broader market dragged the stock lower without any concrete negative company-specific trigger. The reports did not identify a company-specific catalyst for Friday's recovery either.

sum: Siemens and Siemens Healthineers announced on Thursday, November 5, 2026, that the healthcare subsidiary will change its name to Healthineers as part of its planned separation from Siemens. The joint announcement gives Siemens a clearer industrial technology profile while setting a formal milestone for the proposed 2027 spin-off.

Siemens stock traded at 278.80 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 11:08 CET on Thursday, November 5, 1.14 percent above the Xetra close of Wednesday, November 4. The real-time quote of Siemens stock provides the latest market indication.

The proposal would make Healthineers the future name of Siemens Healthineers after deconsolidation. The company said the name change must be approved at the Siemens Healthineers annual shareholders' meeting. The planned spin-off itself is also scheduled to go before the annual shareholders' meetings of both companies in February 2027.

The legal separation will be completed when the spin-off is entered in the German Commercial Register. Only after that step is expected to come the brand migration. Siemens and Healthineers agreed a three-year transition period to support the re-registration of legal entities and products, so the change will unfold gradually rather than through an immediate switch.

Siemens CEO Roland Busch said the move reflects Healthineers' development into a global healthcare leader and sharpens Siemens' profile as a company that scales industrial AI in the real world. The statement links that strategy to Siemens' combination of physical and digital technologies across industry, infrastructure, mobility and healthcare.

For Siemens investors, the announcement separates two strategic questions. Healthineers would gain a distinct identity and shareholder structure, while Siemens would place greater emphasis on industrial businesses and applications that connect the real and digital worlds. The transaction remains subject to shareholder approval and the subsequent legal steps.

Siemens said its fiscal 2025, which ended on September 30, 2025, generated revenue of 78.9 billion euros and net income of 10.4 billion euros. The group employed around 318,000 people on a continuing-operations basis at that date.

sum: Siemens Energy's stock has become a battleground where confidence in the order book collides with hard questions about what investors are already paying for it. Two bullish research houses and one determined bear have staked out positions ahead of the company's full-year 2026 results on 11 November — a date that will also bring fresh medium-term targets, reportedly extending out to 2030.

Bernstein built its recommendation on Siemens Energy's positioning in the electricity supply chain for data centres, a theme that has driven both the stock's recent swings and its recovery. The shares climbed 2.0% in a friendly session for companies seen as beneficiaries of the data centre boom, with media reports pointing to repeated buying in that cohort after an earlier pullback. Strong quarterly results from US rival GE Vernova were cited as a tailwind.

Bank of America had already reaffirmed its buy rating on 29 October, calling the share price decline overdone and pointing to encouraging signals from the figures published by GE Vernova and Hitachi Energy. The two houses agree on direction but not on emphasis: Bernstein leans on the data centre angle, while Bank of America draws on the broader sector read-across. Neither set of peer results is Siemens Energy's own — they sketch the demand backdrop, not the company's performance.

The earlier sell-off, by contrast, was attributed in media reports to a global wave of pressure on AI-related stocks following results from Amazon and Intel. Siemens Energy was caught in the downdraft; no company-specific announcement triggered the move.

mwb Research staked out the opposite corner on 22 October, reiterating its sell rating with a 100 € price target — even while expecting a strong final quarter. That combination is the crux of the disagreement. On the near-term trajectory the two camps need not contradict each other at all. The real argument is valuation: from mwb's standpoint, even solid results can fall short if the share price already discounts exceptionally high expectations.

Bank of America's optimism rests on several operational levers at once — strong margin momentum in the gas business, expectations of higher grid margins, persistently high gas first-fit orders through 2027 and untapped potential in the service business.

sum: Siemens Energy kept its buyback rolling through the final days of October, purchasing 1,337,076 of its own shares between 26 October and 1 November, according to the interim disclosure published yesterday. The latest update marks the sixth such notice since the programme began on 24 September, and it brings the cumulative total repurchased to 5,850,308 shares.

Daily average prices ranged from EUR 122.6675 to EUR 135.7774 — figures that describe the actual conditions of the transactions, not price targets or any company view on what the stock is worth.

That distinction matters for how investors read the news. A buyback notice is a hard record of a capital measure already carried out. Whether the operating outlook justifies current expectations will only emerge from the business figures and guidance.

The next milestone is 11 November 2026, when Siemens Energy will publish its annual results alongside strategic targets through 2030. The completed financial year and the longer-term trajectory will share the agenda that day.

Buybacks do not substitute for that operational reckoning. What counts for shareholders is which expectations management itself confirms — and on multi-year goals especially, analyst forecasts should not be confused with binding company commitments.

The split among analysts shows why the date carries weight: a strong quarter and an attractive valuation are not the same thing. Views on the business must be kept separate from views on the share price.

Bank of America drew encouraging signals on Thursday from results at GE Vernova and Hitachi Energy, pointing to strong gas turbine margins and anticipating higher margins in grid technology. It also flagged robust gas turbine orders stretching to 2027. No new rating or price target was reported alongside that assessment.

sum: Siemens stock traded at 268.08 euros on Lang & Schwarz at 10:35 CET on Monday, November 2, 0.91 percent above the Xetra close of Friday, October 30. The move came as fresh industrial AI discussions added a strategic technology angle ahead of Siemens' next corporate update.

The Herald Business reported on Monday that Siemens Group Chairman Roland Busch and Naver CEO Choi Soo-yeon held a dialogue on industrial AI at the Asia-Pacific German Business Conference in Seoul on Saturday, October 31. The talks focused on combining German engineering with Asian strengths in AI, chips and digital platforms across manufacturing, energy and mobility.

Choi said industrial AI would reach a true tipping point only when small and midsize companies and their suppliers could use it with ease. She also stressed that human oversight becomes more important as AI handles a wider range of tasks. The comments frame adoption as a supply-chain and productivity issue rather than only a software feature.

Busch said industrial AI would create its full value only when deployed safely and reliably in the field and scaled across industries. That emphasis is relevant for Siemens because the group's industrial offering combines automation, software and digital-twin capabilities with applications in physical production environments.

After the dialogue, Siemens executives visited Naver's 1784 headquarters. The companies discussed cases in which Naver's digital-twin technology has been used in industrial settings and explored ways to take those applications into global markets alongside Siemens' industrial solutions. They also considered cooperation involving robotics and robot foundation models.

The discussions build on a June memorandum of understanding between Naver Cloud and Korea Siemens to advance AI transformation in manufacturing. The planned cooperation combines Siemens industrial automation and digital-twin technology with Naver Cloud's AI and cloud infrastructure, while also targeting joint customer development and industry-specific projects.
For investors, the talks reinforce Siemens' positioning in industrial AI but do not by themselves establish additional revenue or earnings.

sum: Siemens Energy shares fell 6.1% on Friday, caught in a widening pullback from artificial intelligence names. For investors, the sell-off raises a question that has less to do with the share price than with the business behind it: can the company still justify expectations built on higher prices and wider margins, or do those forecasts now need trimming?

According to dpa-AFX, doubts about the profitability of multi-billion-dollar AI investments weighed on Siemens Energy alongside its peers. Media reports pointed to Intel's weaker quarterly outlook as an additional drag on AI-linked stocks. The decline is therefore best read as a reaction to the broader market backdrop rather than to any new guidance from Siemens Energy itself.

That distinction matters. A sector-wide loss of confidence can hit companies whose own expectations are unchanged — but it can equally expose assumptions that had gone unchallenged. The price move alone does not settle which reading applies.

The more specific pressure came from Barclays, which according to media reports warned of limited room for further price and margin increases in the energy technology sector. The scepticism is thus not confined to the scale of future data-centre spending. It extends to how much economic benefit suppliers can actually extract from it.

For Siemens Energy shareholders, demand and earnings quality are two separate things. Even if investment keeps flowing, the terms available to equipment makers remain an open question. The risk therefore lies not only in possible project cuts but in assumptions about profitability that may prove too optimistic.

Comments on pricing and margins will carry particular weight at the next set of results. Hard evidence could help separate industry-wide caution from the company's own trajectory. General confidence about demand, by contrast, would not fully answer the concern about a margin ceiling.

The company's ongoing share repurchase belongs in the same assessment. Siemens Energy reported the acquisition of 1,294,334 of its own shares in its latest interim disclosure, covering the period from 19 to 25 October. In total, 4,513,232 shares had been bought back under the programme by that point.

The stock market is not always rational. This is currently very evident in the uranium market. While the AI-energy boom is driving a nuclear power renaissance, uranium stocks are largely on the sidelines. Does this present a huge opportunity for investors? After all, in the US alone, uranium demand is more likely to rise than fall, and the country is already overwhelmingly dependent on imports. American Atomics aims to help change this. American Atomics is particularly optimistic about the development of the US uranium market. The US Department of Energy aims to increase domestic uranium production from the current level of around 2 million pounds to 20 million pounds annually by 2033. American Atomics sees itself as a potentially key component of a future national uranium supply.

At the heart of the strategy is the so-called Big Indian Project in Utah. Supply squeeze: Europe's offshore wind sector sees turbine prices jump 40-45% as manufacturer options shrink
sum: Europe's offshore wind expansion is running into a structural supply constraint where the turbine market is becoming increasingly concentrated. GE Vernova, Siemens Gamesa and Vestas have historically anchored Western offshore turbine supply, but with GE Vernova having paused new offshore wind orders following a series of technical and operational setbacks, Siemens Gamesa and Vestas now account for virtually all turbines available to European developers. Rystad Energy’s analysis of the offshore wind market outlines a sharp increase in per-megawatt (MW) costs, with turbine selling prices rising by between 40% and 45% since 2020, outpacing manufacturing cost increases of 20% to 25% over the same period.

This pricing pressure is most acute in the turbine's most complex components. The nacelle, which houses the generator, gearbox and power electronics that convert wind into electricity, sits at the center of current supply constraints, while similar pressures are emerging in blade manufacturing, driven by increasing turbine sizes, longer production cycles and the logistical demands of transporting and installing next-generation components.

The supply constraint is not evenly distributed across the turbine value chain. It is most pronounced in nacelles and blades, where supplier concentration is high and substitution is limited, while towers remain comparatively more flexible, with a broader supplier base and lower barriers to entry. As a result, the market is becoming increasingly constrained in its most critical components, shaping the overall balance between supply and demand.

Europe's offshore ambitions are real, and the pipeline reflects genuine political commitment. But the market has moved into structurally tight territory: high demand, limited supplier diversity and rising turbine complexity. That combination gives original equipment manufacturers (OEM) real pricing power and the ability to be selective about which projects get built.

sum: Artificial intelligence (AI) technology has taken the stock market by storm in recent years, driving solid growth for several companies involved in its development and distribution.

Not surprisingly, many AI stocks have created significant wealth for investors in recent years. From Nvidia (NVDA -4.63%) to Palantir Technologies, Broadcom, or Micron Technology, AI has minted multiple high-flying stocks. The good news is that AI adoption is poised to take off in the long run. A third-party estimate pegs the size of the AI market at a whopping $5.3 trillion in 2035, up from $274 billion in 2023.

As a result, it won't be surprising to see AI generate generational wealth for investors in the long run, helping them build enough capital to pass down to their descendants. That's why we are going to take a closer look at Nvidia, a tech giant with the potential to create generational wealth.
AI could make Nvidia a much bigger company than it is right now

Nvidia is one of the biggest names in AI right now. Its chips have played a critical role in training AI models and in inference applications. The outstanding demand for its chips has made Nvidia the world's largest company by market cap. But what's worth noting is that Nvidia still has room to grow despite reaching a $4.4 trillion market cap.

The company finished its 2026 fiscal year (which ended on Jan. 25, 2026) with almost $216 billion in revenue, up 65% from the prior year. What's worth noting is that Nvidia's $78 billion revenue outlook for the current quarter calls for a 77% year-over-year increase, suggesting that it is poised for an acceleration despite its massive revenue base.

There are a few solid reasons why Nvidia is still capable of growing at an incredible rate. The first is that the global AI chip market could grow from an estimated $500 billion in 2026 to $1 trillion in 2030, a compound annual growth rate of almost 19%. Nvidia is the dominant player in this market, with an estimated 90% share, and its growth rate suggests it can sustain its dominance.

sum: Siemens Energy secured a sizable commercial win this week, agreeing to supply Dynamis Power Solutions with 119 SGT-400 gas turbine cores. Each unit delivers roughly 15 megawatts, and the first batch is scheduled to ship in 2027.

The deal matters because it underscores a quieter truth about the business: while the industry's imagination is captured by futuristic technologies, the bread-and-butter turbine segment keeps delivering dependable earnings. Demand for decentralized power generation remains robust, and this contract locks in valuable capacity utilization for years to come.

Sentiment around the stock also received a lift from RBC, which added Siemens Energy to its "Top 30 Global Ideas for 2026" list. RBC's case rests on expectations through 2030: average annual revenue growth of 13 percent and an average increase of 40 percent in adjusted operating profit (EBITA).
Shares closed Friday at 145.56 euros, up 1.1 percent on the session — still some distance from the 52-week high of 195.38 euros, but with the fundamental backdrop visibly brightening.

Before the RBC note, the stock had come under pressure amid a broad pullback in AI infrastructure names. Worries about a possible cooling in data-center investment, along with debates over tighter safety regulations, weighed on the sector. Warnings from Anthropic chief Dario Amodei were cited as one backdrop for that caution. Notably, the dip was not driven by any operational setback at Siemens Energy itself.

The episode illustrates how sensitive the energy sector has become to developments in the digital economy. Rising electricity demand from technology facilities ranks among the most important growth fields, yet it also leaves related stocks exposed to swings in the tech sector.

The new order slots neatly into the picture management painted during its latest pre-close call. For fiscal 2026, the company is sticking to its forecast of comparable revenue growth in a range of 14 to 16 percent. That confidence, in my view, signals that execution on the existing order book is proceeding according to plan — and that management retains the composure to keep its ambitious profitability targets in sight.

items.t: Siemens Energy Insiders Put Money on the Line as Shares Drift From Peak
sum: A Siemens Energy supervisory board member has backed the company with a personal outlay of roughly €100,000, even as the stock trades well below its 52-week high and a swirl of market noise — from SpaceX speculation to rising bond yields — keeps the shares under pressure.

Laurence Mulliez, who sits on the energy technology group's supervisory board, acquired 660 shares at €151.91 apiece in late August, a transaction disclosed to Germany's financial regulator BaFin as an insider trade. Board-level purchases of this kind are often read by investors as a signal of conviction, since they commit personal capital without any obligation to publicise the move.

The timing is notable. The buy came after the stock had already retreated meaningfully from its record high of €195.38. At the current price of around €144, the shares sit roughly 4.9 percent below their 200-day moving average of €151.37 — evidence that the medium-term uptrend has flattened, even if the twelve-month performance remains firmly positive.

The market's recent skittishness traces back to reports that SpaceX is weighing in-house production of gas turbine components, a prospect that briefly knocked the stock to €139.50 on Thursday before it recovered. Analysts have been quick to pour cold water on the idea, pointing out that gas turbines account for only about ten percent of Siemens Energy's group revenue — hardly a scale that makes an immediate competitive threat existential.

JPMorgan reaffirmed its "Overweight" rating with a €245 price target in early September, with analyst Phil Buller arguing that SpaceX's plans appear aimed at individual components rather than a full entry into gas turbine manufacturing. RBC trimmed its target from €210 to €200 in late August but kept an "Outperform" stance, framing the adjustment as a recalibration of earnings expectations rather than operational doubt. Jefferies also shaved its target, to €210, while stressing that weakness in the gas turbine business stems from extended supply chains, not softening demand.

sum: Siemens shares gained 3 per cent as analysts remained positive after the September quarter topline beat the street's estimates, even as profit fell
Shares of Siemens Ltd. rose over 3 per cent on Monday as analysts remained positive after the September quarter topline beat the street's estimates despite a profit decline.

The heavy electrical equipment maker's stock rose as much as 3.31 per cent during the day to ₹3,186.3 per share, the biggest intraday rise since October 6 this year. The stock pared gains to trade 2.3 per cent higher at ₹3,156 apiece, compared to a 0.23 per cent advance in Nifty 50 as of 10:00 AM.

Shares of the company rose for the fourth straight session and currently trade at 8.9 times the average 30-day trading volume, according to Bloomberg. The counter has fallen 7 per cent this year, compared to a 9.8 per cent advance in the benchmark Nifty 50. Siemens has a total market capitalisation of ₹1.12 trillion.

Siemens has reported over 7 per cent year-on-year (y-o-y) decline in consolidated net profit to ₹485 crore for the quarter ended September 30, 2025. However, the company saw its revenue from operations grow 16 per cent to ₹5,171 crore during the quarter under review from ₹4,457 crore in the year-ago period.

"We delivered a robust performance this quarter, with a surge in revenue, driven by strong performance in our mobility and smart infrastructure businesses, while digital Industries volumes were impacted due to a lower reach in the order backlog from the previous year and muted private sector capex," managing director and chief executive officer, Sunil Mathur, said.

Siemens's topline exceeded estimates by 8 per cent, though the Ebitda beat was a modest 5 per cent due to demerger-related costs, according to JM Financial. The brokerage said profit after tax was ahead of expectations by just 2 per cent, as higher tax outgo and lower other income weighed on the bottom line.
